paragraphs.heading: Fighting from a ditch
paragraphs.text: Trench warfare is a way of fighting on land from occupied lines that are made up mostly of military trenches. Inside them, soldiers are well shielded from enemy fire and largely protected from artillery. Armies used trenches in ancient times, but the method only fully took shape in the 17th century.

paragraphs.heading: Trenches in the ancient world
paragraphs.text: The Greek historian Thucydides mentioned trenches as early as the 5th century B.C., in his history of the Peloponnesian War. Roman writers such as Polybius and Flavius Josephus also described them. The fullest account comes from Caesar, who wrote about the trenches built at the Siege of Alesia. Until the early modern period, trenches were mostly obstacles in the enemy's path, sometimes filled with water.

paragraphs.heading: Zigzags and parallels
paragraphs.text: In the 17th century the Ottomans worked out a system of parallels and saps, the saps being trenches that zigzagged toward the enemy. Placing all the infantry in these trenches was meant to protect the besieging side from the defenders' artillery. Later in that century the French military engineer Vauban took up the system. His plan used three parallel trenches joined by zigzag approach trenches, usually four to five feet deep.

paragraphs.heading: A preview in America
paragraphs.text: In the American Civil War of 1861 to 1865, especially at the sieges of Vicksburg and Petersburg, modern firepower ran into old-fashioned infantry tactics. Soldiers started digging in to escape the deadly shelling, a change that marked the end of the classic battle in open fields. The trenches were wide enough to sit or stand in, with raised logs in front to guard the heads and shoulders of men firing. Deep holes called bomb-proofs, braced with tree trunks and covered with wood and earth, sheltered troops from bombardment.

paragraphs.heading: The Western Front freezes
paragraphs.text: By 1914, quick-firing guns, machine guns and exploding shells gave defenders a huge edge over advancing infantry and cavalry. After the First Battle of the Aisne, each side kept trying to get around the other's flank in the 'Race to the Sea'. The result was one unbroken line of trenches from Switzerland to the North Sea. By late October 1914 the Western Front had locked into a stalemate, a war of attrition.

paragraphs.heading: Why the deadlock was so deadly
paragraphs.text: With no open flank to go around, armies had no choice but to make costly attacks straight at the enemy. Casualties were massive among attackers and defenders alike as reserves were thrown into counter-attacks and the guns kept firing. Machine guns, rapid-fire artillery and barbed wire held the lines in place, and the trench now decided the whole course of the war. This static fighting lasted until the German Spring Offensive of March 1918, and similar conditions arose in Italy and at Gallipoli.
